title: The whole Christ celebrates (CCC 1136–1144)
hookLine: heaven and earth, priest and people, all take part

lines: A FEW PEOPLE, ROWS OF WOOD.
cards: A weekday morning Mass in a big church that's mostly empty. A priest at the altar. A woman in the front pew with a worn prayer book.
A man near the back who came in on his way to work and kept his coat on. A teenager doing the readings, a little too fast. Rows and rows of empty wood.
It looks like a small gathering. The Catechism sees something else: in its picture, that room is packed.

teach.b: The Catechism says the liturgy is the action of the whole Christ. It even gives the Latin, Christus totus: Christ the head, and his body, the Church, together. So who's there?
In the Apocalypse, John is shown worship already going on in heaven: a throne, a Lamb "standing as it were slain," angels, elders, and every creature praising God.
The living creatures there never stop saying, in the Douay-Rheims: "Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come."
When the Church celebrates on earth, the Catechism teaches, it joins that heavenly liturgy, already in progress.
At Mass, as the great prayer over the bread and wine gets under way, the people sing holy, holy, holy, words close to what the angels sing in the prophet Isaiah.

teach.h: THE SAINTS AND THE WHOLE COMMUNITY.
teach.b: Second, the saints: Mary, the apostles, the martyrs and a great crowd of saints take part. Third, the whole community on earth.
It's not the priest alone who celebrates, the Catechism says, but the whole body of Christ, united with its head. Every baptized person shares in it.
Fourth, each in their own role. The ordained priest acts in a particular way, in the person of Christ. But readers, servers and singers all have a real part, and all of it is one act.

So, back to that weekday morning: a priest, a woman with a prayer book, a man in a coat, a nervous reader, and, in the Catholic understanding, angels, saints and the whole Church. Not a small gathering. A full house.

how: At Mass Catholics sing or say the Holy, holy, holy after the preface, near the start of the Eucharistic Prayer, which the Church understands as joining the praise of the angels and saints in heaven.

games.q: what does “the whole christ celebrates” mean?
o: the priest alone offering worship for the people
Christ and his whole body, heaven and earth, at worship
a Mass held only on the greatest feast days

games.q: the whole Christ — tap the pairs.
p: Christ the head, and his body
a real part in the liturgy

s: the Catechism says the priest alone celebrates the liturgy
it says the whole community, the body of Christ united with its head, celebrates.
the holy, holy, holy at Mass echoes the angels' words in Isaiah
the Church on earth joins the worship already going on in heaven.
a weekday Mass with a handful of people is a small liturgy
the Catechism's picture includes angels, saints and the whole Church.

games.q: you're at a weekday Mass with a handful of people in a big empty church. who, in the Catechism's picture, is taking part?
o: the handful of people in the pews
Christ, the angels, the saints and the whole Church
games.why: the Catechism calls the liturgy the act of the whole Christ, head and body, joined to the worship already going on in heaven.

practice: Let the room around you get bigger in your mind: somewhere right now, people are gathered to pray, in big churches and small chapels, in hospitals, in kitchens.
If you pray, join them slowly with the angels' words from Isaiah, holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts, knowing you aren't saying them alone.
If you don't, simply sit with the thought that others, somewhere, are reaching toward something larger than themselves.

wordCard.voice: The whole Christ celebrates. Catholics believe the liturgy is the act of Christ and his whole body: heaven and earth, priest and people, angels and saints, all taking part. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the whole Christ, head and body together. The Catechism uses it for who celebrates the liturgy.

carryVoice: Your line: all of us. Head and body, heaven and earth, together. See you tomorrow.
